definition: Evince means to show or reveal clearly.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word evince. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know evince should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The old workbench itself evinces decades of careful habits: every tool outlined in paint, every drawer sliding without a squeak.
To imply is to leave a trace for the alert reader; it stops well short of evince, which puts the quality on open display.
Prove goes further than imply on this ladder — proof settles the question beyond argument, while what is evinced is clearly shown yet still short of demonstrated.

To reveal is the everyday verb for bringing anything hidden into view — a face, a secret, a price. To evince is narrower and more formal: conduct or evidence puts an inner quality on open display, the way a steady voice under pressure shows composure.

To betray a feeling is to reveal it without meaning to — the tremor gives the speaker away. To evince carries no such accident: the quality is simply there to be seen in the evidence, whether or not its owner minds.

With both champions injured, the team that had seemed invincible finally lost.
Evince means to show or reveal clearly.
Buyers toured the orchard for an hour, and the ledgers evinced what the owner never said aloud: replanted rows after the blight, drainage dug in the wet years, a decade of patient spending on soil.
The farm's history of care was legible in the numbers.
Evince means the evidence makes something inner or hidden plainly visible — attitudes, qualities, feelings.
It is stronger than hint, but it stops short of prove: what is evinced is shown clearly, not demonstrated beyond argument.
Evince lives in reports, reviews and letters of reference: conduct evinces a quality.
Use reveal for everyday showing, betray when the showing is accidental, and prove when the evidence settles the matter.
People evince composure; documents evince care; nobody evinces a kitchen.
